scenes.text: Say your own name. Out loud. Now say it again — and again — thirty times, until your tongue starts tripping over it.
Somewhere around the twentieth, something goes sideways. The name stops being yours. It's just a sound. A little noise your mouth makes.
That's not you losing it. That's a glitch with a name. Jamais vu — the opposite of deja vu. Instead of the strange feeling familiar, the familiar goes strange.
And underneath the label? The raw thing. The actual noise. The strangeness that was sitting there the whole time — just covered.
Stare long enough and it becomes an object you happen to be wearing.
It's a small vertigo, isn't it? The floor of the ordinary drops out. And for one second you're a stranger in your own kitchen, holding a fork you've never seen before.
Here's the part I love. People spend real money chasing this feeling. The world made new, the veil lifted. And it was free the whole time — built right into the hardware.
Because the familiarity was never in the thing. It was in you — a habit of prediction laid over the top so smoothly you mistook it for the world.
Wonder isn't a place you have to travel to. It's a glitch. And you can trigger it on purpose — in a chair, with a single word.
So here's the test. Look at your own hand until it turns back into an object. That astonishment — it was always available. You just never stared long enough to be surprised.
